questions.question: Q1. Define significant figures. State any two rules.
questions.answer: Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a measured value. Rules: all non-zero digits are significant; zeros between significant digits are significant; leading zeros are not significant; trailing zeros after a decimal are significant.
questions.shortcut: Count every non-zero digit; keep internal & decimal-point trailing zeros; drop leading zeros.

questions.question: Q2. State the difference between precision and accuracy with an example.
questions.answer: Precision = closeness of repeated measurements to each other. Accuracy = closeness to the true value. A value can be precise but inaccurate (consistent wrong) or accurate but imprecise.
questions.shortcut: Precision → spread; Accuracy → distance from true value.
questions.example: Repeated 4.2,4.3,4.1 g is precise; if true is 5.0 g it is not accurate.

questions.question: Q3. What is a fundamental (base) unit? Give SI base units of two quantities.
questions.answer: A fundamental unit is the standard unit of a fundamental quantity independent of others. Examples: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature).
questions.shortcut: 7 SI base units: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd.

questions.question: Q4. Define parallax error and how it is avoided.
questions.answer: Parallax error is the apparent shift between the pointer and the scale reading because the eye is not directly above the scale. Avoid it by placing a mirror below the scale or keeping the eye perpendicular to the scale at the point of reading. ▥ 1.1 Precision, Significant Figures & Units  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Precision vs Accuracy (classic contrast) Fundamental vs Derived Quantities ▣ 1.2 Dimensions & Dimensional Analysis
questions.shortcut: Eye ⟂ to scale, eye-line on the pointer.
questions.example: Galvanometer/scale with a mirror → read when image of pointer overlaps pointer.

questions.question: Q5. Define dimensional analysis. State two uses.
questions.answer: Dimensional analysis expresses a physical quantity as a product of powers of base dimensions M, L, T. Uses: (i) verify dimensional homogeneity of an equation, (ii) find the dimensions of a quantity, (iii) convert units, (iv) derive a relation among quantities.
questions.shortcut: Write the formula, replace each symbol by M,L,T powers, simplify exponents.

questions.question: Q6. Write dimensional formulas of velocity, pressure and torque.
questions.answer: Velocity [v]=LT⁻¹. Pressure [P]=ML⁻¹T⁻². Torque [τ]=M L² T⁻² (force × lever arm).
questions.shortcut: velocity L/T; pressure F/area; torque like energy ML²T⁻².
questions.example: Note torque and energy share M L² T⁻² but differ (torque is a vector).

questions.question: Q7. Verify dimensionally that [Work] = [torque].
questions.answer: Work = force × displacement = MLT⁻²·L = ML²T⁻². Torque = force × arm = MLT⁻²·L = ML²T⁻². Both = ML²T⁻², hence dimensionally equal.
questions.shortcut: Both reduce to force × length → ML²T⁻².

questions.question: Q8. State two limitations of dimensional analysis.
questions.answer: (i) It cannot verify relations involving addition/subtraction or trigonometric/logarithmic functions. (ii) It cannot find numerical constants, and it gives no information about vectors vs scalars (torque & energy have same dimensions).
questions.shortcut: Dimensional analysis fails for +, −, sin, log, and constants (like ½).
questions.example: v = u + at is verified term-by-term, not the whole sum at once.

questions.question: Q9. Find the dimensions of G using Newton's law of gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r².
questions.example: SI unit of G: N·m²/kg² = m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻².

questions.question: Q10. Verify dimensionally E = ½ m v².
questions.answer: RHS = mass × velocity² = M(LT⁻¹)² = ML²T⁻². Energy [E] = work = ML²T⁻². LHS = RHS, so the equation is dimensionally correct (constant ½ is ignored). ▥ 1.2 Dimensions & Dimensional Analysis  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Dimensions of Common Quantities (quick lookup) What Dimensional Analysis Can / Cannot Do PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.shortcut: ½ is dimensionless; check only M,L,T.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the dimensions of the gravitational constant G.
theoryItems.answer: From F = Gm₁m₂/r²: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂). Dimensions = (MLT⁻²)(L²)/M² = M⁻¹L³T⁻².

theoryItems.question: [State] T2. Define accuracy and precision; how are they different?
theoryItems.answer: Accuracy = closeness to the true value (systematic errors matter). Precision = reproducibility of repeated readings (random error / least-count). A result can be precise but inaccurate (consistent bias) or accurate but imprecise (scattered, mean ≈ true).
theoryItems.shortcut: Precise = small spread; Accurate = near true value.
theoryItems.example: Repeated 4.2,4.1,4.3 g is precise; if true = 5.0 g it is not accurate.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. List the seven SI base units with their quantities.
theoryItems.answer: Length–metre, mass–kilogram, time–second, current–ampere, temperature–kelvin, amount–mole, luminous intensity–candela. These are independent (fundamental); all others are derived.
theoryItems.shortcut: 7 base: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd.
theoryItems.example: SI units are the international standard for all measurements.

theoryItems.question: [State] T4. What is a derived unit? Give two with dimensions.
theoryItems.answer: Derived units are formed by combining base units. Pressure = N/m² = Pa → ML⁻¹T⁻²; Energy = N·m = J → ML²T⁻².
theoryItems.shortcut: Write quantity → replace by M,L,T powers.

theoryItems.question: [Compare] T5. Compare systematic and random errors; how is each reduced?
theoryItems.answer: Systematic: one-sided, due to instrument bias (zero error, calibration) → reduce by calibration & correcting zero. Random: scatter about the true value from fluctuating conditions → reduce by repeating and averaging, guarding against parallax.
theoryItems.example: A biased ruler = systematic; shaky hand = random.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain the method of finding the density of a solid by a spring balance + water (displacement).
theoryItems.answer: Weigh the solid in air (m₁). Submerge it in water and weigh (m₂, apparent weight). Upthrust = (m₁−m₂)g = weight of displaced water = V·ρ_w·g → Volume V = (m₁−m₂)/ρ_w. Density = m₁/V = m₁ρ_w/(m₁−m₂).
theoryItems.example: A 50 g stone displacing 20 cm³ water → ρ = 2.5 g/cm³.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain the use of a Vernier scale (least count). How is the reading taken?
theoryItems.answer: A Vernier scale subdivides the main scale: least count = 1 main-division / N vernier-divisions. Reading = whole main scale + (vernier division coinciding × least count).

theoryItems.question: [Why] T8. Why do we express a final answer with the correct number of significant figures?
theoryItems.answer: To reflect the precision of the least-precise measurement: propagating more digits than the data support gives a false sense of accuracy. The answer's significant figures match the least-precise input.

theoryItems.question: [Viva] T9. A professor asks: 'If I double the length and halve the cross-section of a wire, what happens to its resistance? What law tells me?'
theoryItems.answer: R = ρL/A. Doubling L and halving A makes R increase by 4× (L↑×2, A↓×2 → R×4). This is the resistance (resistivity) law.
theoryItems.example: ρ is a material property, L and A geometry.

▣ 1.1 Precision, Significant Figures & Units
Q1. Define significant figures. State any two rules.

Answer:  Significant figures are the meaningful digits in a measured value. Rules: all non-zero digits are significant; zeros between significant digits are significant; leading zeros are not significant; trailing zeros after a decimal are significant.
⚡ Shortcut:  Count every non-zero digit; keep internal & decimal-point trailing zeros; drop leading zeros.
Example:  0.004050 → 4 significant figures (4,0,5,0).
Q2. State the difference between precision and accuracy with an example.
Answer:  Precision = closeness of repeated measurements to each other. Accuracy = closeness to the true value. A value can be precise but inaccurate (consistent wrong) or accurate but imprecise.
⚡ Shortcut:  Precision → spread; Accuracy → distance from true value.
Example:  Repeated 4.2,4.3,4.1 g is precise; if true is 5.0 g it is not accurate.
Q3. What is a fundamental (base) unit? Give SI base units of two quantities.
Answer:  A fundamental unit is the standard unit of a fundamental quantity independent of others. Examples: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (current), kelvin (temperature).
⚡ Shortcut:  7 SI base units: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd.
Example:  Mass = kilogram, time = second.
Q4. Define parallax error and how it is avoided.

Answer:  Parallax error is the apparent shift between the pointer and the scale reading because the eye is not directly above the scale. Avoid it by placing a mirror below the scale or keeping the eye perpendicular to the scale at the point of reading.
⚡ Shortcut:  Eye ⟂ to scale, eye-line on the pointer.
Example:  Galvanometer/scale with a mirror → read when image of pointer overlaps pointer.

▣ 1.2 Dimensions & Dimensional Analysis
Q5. Define dimensional analysis. State two uses.

Answer:  Dimensional analysis expresses a physical quantity as a product of powers of base dimensions M, L, T. Uses: (i) verify dimensional homogeneity of an equation, (ii) find the dimensions of a quantity, (iii) convert units, (iv) derive a relation among quantities.
⚡ Shortcut:  Write the formula, replace each symbol by M,L,T powers, simplify exponents.
Example:  Dimension of pressure = [F/A] = MLT⁻²/L² = ML⁻¹T⁻².
Q6. Write dimensional formulas of velocity, pressure and torque.
Answer:  Velocity [v]=LT⁻¹. Pressure [P]=ML⁻¹T⁻². Torque [τ]=M L² T⁻² (force × lever arm).
⚡ Shortcut:  velocity L/T; pressure F/area; torque like energy ML²T⁻².
Example:  Note torque and energy share M L² T⁻² but differ (torque is a vector).
Q7. Verify dimensionally that [Work] = [torque].
Answer:  Work = force × displacement = MLT⁻²·L = ML²T⁻². Torque = force × arm = MLT⁻²·L = ML²T⁻². Both = ML²T⁻², hence dimensionally equal.
⚡ Shortcut:  Both reduce to force × length → ML²T⁻².
Example:  Unit of both: joule (N·m).
Q8. State two limitations of dimensional analysis.

Answer:  (i) It cannot verify relations involving addition/subtraction or trigonometric/logarithmic functions. (ii) It cannot find numerical constants, and it gives no information about vectors vs scalars (torque & energy have same dimensions).
⚡ Shortcut:  Dimensional analysis fails for +, −, sin, log, and constants (like ½).
Example:  v = u + at is verified term-by-term, not the whole sum at once.
Q9. Find the dimensions of G using Newton's law of gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r².
Answer:  G = Fr²/(m₁m₂). Dimensions = (MLT⁻²)(L²)/M² = M⁻¹L³T⁻².
⚡ Shortcut:  G = F L² / M² → M⁻¹L³T⁻².
Example:  SI unit of G: N·m²/kg² = m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻².
Q10. Verify dimensionally E = ½ m v².
Answer:  RHS = mass × velocity² = M(LT⁻¹)² = ML²T⁻². Energy [E] = work = ML²T⁻². LHS = RHS, so the equation is dimensionally correct (constant ½ is ignored).
⚡ Shortcut:  ½ is dimensionless; check only M,L,T.
Example:  Same check confirms kinetic-energy formula.

▹ Derive  (derivations & long answers)
[Derive] T1. Derive the dimensions of the gravitational constant G.
Answer:  From F = Gm₁m₂/r²: G = Fr²/(m₁m₂). Dimensions = (MLT⁻²)(L²)/M² = M⁻¹L³T⁻².
⚡ Short / exam line:  G = F L² / M².
Example:  SI unit: N·m²/kg² = m³kg⁻¹s⁻².
▹ State  (definitions, laws & formulae)
[State] T2. Define accuracy and precision; how are they different?

Answer:  Accuracy = closeness to the true value (systematic errors matter). Precision = reproducibility of repeated readings (random error / least-count). A result can be precise but inaccurate (consistent bias) or accurate but imprecise (scattered, mean ≈ true).
⚡ Short / exam line:  Precise = small spread; Accurate = near true value.
Example:  Repeated 4.2,4.1,4.3 g is precise; if true = 5.0 g it is not accurate.
[State] T3. List the seven SI base units with their quantities.
Answer:  Length–metre, mass–kilogram, time–second, current–ampere, temperature–kelvin, amount–mole, luminous intensity–candela. These are independent (fundamental); all others are derived.
⚡ Short / exam line:  7 base: m, kg, s, A, K, mol, cd.
Example:  SI units are the international standard for all measurements.
[State] T4. What is a derived unit? Give two with dimensions.
Answer:  Derived units are formed by combining base units. Pressure = N/m² = Pa → ML⁻¹T⁻²; Energy = N·m = J → ML²T⁻².
⚡ Short / exam line:  Write quantity → replace by M,L,T powers.
Example:  Force (N), power (W) are also derived.
▹ Compare  (compare & contrast)
[Compare] T5. Compare systematic and random errors; how is each reduced?

Answer:  Systematic: one-sided, due to instrument bias (zero error, calibration) → reduce by calibration & correcting zero. Random: scatter about the true value from fluctuating conditions → reduce by repeating and averaging, guarding against parallax.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Systematic = offset; Random = scatter.
Example:  A biased ruler = systematic; shaky hand = random.
▹ Explain  (working / principle / application)
[Explain] T6. Explain the method of finding the density of a solid by a spring balance + water (displacement).

Answer:  Weigh the solid in air (m₁). Submerge it in water and weigh (m₂, apparent weight). Upthrust = (m₁−m₂)g = weight of displaced water = V·ρ_w·g → Volume V = (m₁−m₂)/ρ_w. Density = m₁/V = m₁ρ_w/(m₁−m₂).
⚡ Short / exam line:  V = displaced volume; ρ = m/V (Archimedes).
Example:  A 50 g stone displacing 20 cm³ water → ρ = 2.5 g/cm³.
[Explain] T7. Explain the use of a Vernier scale (least count). How is the reading taken?
Answer:  A Vernier scale subdivides the main scale: least count = 1 main-division / N vernier-divisions. Reading = whole main scale + (vernier division coinciding × least count).
⚡ Short / exam line:  L.C. = MSD/N; reading = M + (v×L.C.).
Example:  LC = 0.01 mm; reading 12 mm + (35×0.01)=12.35 mm.
▹ Why  (conceptual & 'why' questions)
[Why] T8. Why do we express a final answer with the correct number of significant figures?

Answer:  To reflect the precision of the least-precise measurement: propagating more digits than the data support gives a false sense of accuracy. The answer's significant figures match the least-precise input.
⚡ Short / exam line:  Match sig-figs to least-precise term.
Example:  3.0 (2 s.f.) × 2.50 (3 s.f.) → answer to 2 s.f.
▹ Viva  (viva-voce probing)
[Viva] T9. A professor asks: 'If I double the length and halve the cross-section of a wire, what happens to its resistance? What law tells me?'
Answer:  R = ρL/A. Doubling L and halving A makes R increase by 4× (L↑×2, A↓×2 → R×4). This is the resistance (resistivity) law.
⚡ Short / exam line:  R ∝ L/A → 4×.
Example:  ρ is a material property, L and A geometry.
